text: Every company has a Dave. And when Dave leaves, everything he knew walks out the door with him. I've worked at a bunch of private companies, and the hardest thing for all of them wasn't sales or hiring. It was writing down what people know. At one place, our most senior engineer left on a Friday. By Monday, nobody knew how half the system worked. [chuckles] We spent weeks piecing it back together from old emails and chat messages. Someone leaves, and years of context are just gone. And the docs that do exist, stale. Nobody trusts them. [sighs] So people just ask each other over and over. So I tried fixing it for myself first. Obsidian, Notion, all of them. And honestly, the graphs are gorgeous, but making them is so tedious. Every note, you're linking things by hand. [chuckles] It turns into a second job. I always wished it would just do that for me. So I built it. It's called Corpus Wiki. You just feed it PDFs, Word docs, notes, screenshots, even videos, or connect your Gmail. It pulls out the facts and writes the wiki for you, every line linked to where it came from. And it connects everything: the graph, the glossary, who's who, automatically. No brackets, ever. Ask it anything, like, "Why did we switch payment providers?" And it answers from what your team actually wrote, with sources. Drop in a newer file, and it only rewrites the lines that changed. And if two files disagree, it asks you first. A normal wiki only knows what someone remembered to write down. This one keeps up on its own. And when someone leaves, what they knew stays. Dave's knowledge? [chuckles] Still here. I've been testing it with a few teams, and people are pretty surprised how much it remembers. If your team keeps losing knowledge or you're tired of linking notes by hand, try it. Drop in a folder and watch it build your brain. Link's below.
